stances.claim: Despite Trump's baseless suits, shameless shenanigans, chaotic mobs, and incited rioters, Congress certified Biden as the new president -- a 'fitting conclusion' to the dismissal of Trump's 50+ post-election suits by federal and state courts including the Scotus.

Trump's political shenanigans escalated through Mike Flynn's martial-law call, the Raffensperger 'find 11,780 votes' demand with criminal-charge threats, and the request that Pence undermine the congressional certification -- but none succeeded.

Unlike the Philippines, the US lacks an independent nonpartisan Comelec equivalent, privately-run nonpartisan election watchdogs (PPCRV, Namfrel), and a Presidential Electoral Tribunal; 50 states regulate their own elections, and chief election officers are usually elected partisan officials.

Despite these obvious structural gaps, US elections have been comparatively peaceful, orderly, and credible -- because partisan election officers nonetheless faithfully follow election laws and do not invent facts to fit their political biases (Raffensperger as the example).

Concrete examples of US institutional resistance: Raffensperger's defiance; Pence's textual constitutional rebuff; the 10 living former defense secretaries' joint letter blocking any military intervention; the affirmative vote of three Trump-appointed Scotus justices dismissing Trump's suit on short shrift.

First, without constitutional safeguards or private sentinels, the US held a credible election sans lengthy post-election protests; second, Trump did his worst and American democracy still prevailed -- and the question is: 'Can we do the same?'

notable_anecdotes: The Raffensperger numerical detail -- Trump asking him to 'find 11,780 votes' to overturn Biden's 'lead of 11,779 votes' (i.e., flip by exactly one ballot) with threats of criminal charges if he refused -- the most damning single political fact in the column, the precise arithmetic of the demand exposing its naked illegitimacy.

The triple-count Georgia detail -- 'ballots had been counted three times, the last one, manually, at Trump's request, and the result was the same' -- a quiet refutation through procedural exhaustiveness.
Raffensperger's direct quote -- 'President Trump... We don't agree that you have won' -- embedded as the column's central institutional resistance line.

Pence's constitutional self-restraint -- 'The Constitution constrains me from claiming unilateral authority to determine which electoral votes should be counted and which should not' -- set up as the Vice President textually rebuking his own President's request.

The 10 former defense secretaries' joint letter (with two Trump-era signatories) -- explicitly preempting any military intervention in the electoral controversy -- used to illustrate cross-administration institutional unity.
The three Trump-appointed Scotus justices voting to dismiss Trump's suit 'on short shrift' -- the structurally most embarrassing single fact for Trump, his own appointees refusing the favor.
The closing interrogative -- 'Can we do the same?' -- pointed back at the Philippine reader, turning a column about the US into a domestic challenge.

one_paragraph_summary: Despite Trump's baseless suits, shameless shenanigans, chaotic mobs, and incited rioters, the US Congress certified Joe Biden's 306-232 Electoral College victory -- a 'fitting conclusion' to the dismissal of more than 50 Trump post-election suits by federal and state courts including the Supreme Court of the United States. Panganiban inventories the escalating shenanigans: Trump's denunciation of absentee voting while ironically using a Florida absentee ballot; Mike Flynn's unprecedented call for martial law and a re-staging of the 2020 election; the now-infamous Raffensperger call demanding 11,780 votes to flip Biden's 11,779-vote lead in Georgia by a single ballot, with criminal-charge threats; and the request that VP Pence undermine the congressional certification. He then turns to a structural comparison: unlike the Philippines, the US has no independent nonpartisan Comelec, no PPCRV or Namfrel watchdogs, no Presidential Electoral Tribunal -- 50 states regulate their own elections, and chief election officers are usually elected partisan secretaries of state. Yet despite these structural gaps, US elections have been comparatively peaceful, orderly, and credible because partisan officers nonetheless follow the law and do not invent facts to suit their biases. Concrete examples of institutional resistance: Raffensperger's 'President Trump... We don't agree that you have won' after a thrice-counted (once-manually-at-Trump's-request) ballot; the Jan 5 Georgia Senate runoff returning two Democrats and giving VP Harris a 50-50 tie-breaking vote; Pence's textual constitutional rebuff ('The Constitution constrains me from claiming unilateral authority'); the 10 living former US secretaries of defense (two from Trump's own term) declaring no military role in resolving the election; and the affirmative vote of three Trump-appointed Scotus justices dismissing his suit on short shrift. CJ closes with a two-line ordinal summary and a comparative challenge to the Philippine reader: without constitutional safeguards or private sentinels, the US still produced a credible election; Trump did his worst, and American democracy still prevailed -- 'Can we do the same?'
